Differential forms: construction, projection and operations ​

Introduction ​

Mantis represents every field as a differential form: a function is a 0-form, a quantity that is integrated along curves (such as a circulation) is a 1-form, a quantity integrated over surfaces (such as a flux) is an (n−1)-form, and a density integrated over volumes is an n-form. Why this language is used, and how it relates to the familiar ∇, ∇× and ∇⋅, is explained on the differential forms theory page. The Forms module that implements them is described on the Forms page.

This example shows how to use the Forms module, building on the geometries of the Geometry example and the B-spline spaces of the Function Spaces example. We will:

  1. construct forms of every rank in 1D, 2D and 3D from function spaces and coefficients, and from analytical expressions;

  2. export forms to VTK files to visualize them;

  3. compute the L2 projection of analytical forms onto finite element forms, on coarse and fine meshes and on a curved geometry;

  4. apply the exterior derivative d, the Hodge star ⋆ and the wedge product ∧ to finite element forms, and compare the results with the exact ones.

Constructing forms ​

Form spaces and form fields ​

On a geometry of manifold dimension n, with the parametric coordinates x^=(x^1,…,x^n) of the Geometry example, a k-form has (nk) components, one per basis k-form dx^i1∧⋯∧dx^ik. We write ωck for the c-th basis k-form, in the order used by Mantis:

n1-forms2-forms3-forms
1dx^1
2dx^1, dx^2dx^1∧dx^2
3dx^1, dx^2, dx^3dx^2∧dx^3, dx^3∧dx^1, dx^1∧dx^2dx^1∧dx^2∧dx^3

For example, a 1-form in 2D and a 2-form in 3D are

α1=a1dx^1+a2dx^2,α2=a1dx^2∧dx^3+a2dx^3∧dx^1+a3dx^1∧dx^2.

In Mantis, a finite element form is built in two steps.

Form spaces. Forms.FormSpace(k, space, label) combines a function space with the basis k-forms. The function space must have one component per component of the form, that is, for each c=1,…,(nk), a set of scalar basis functions B^c,1,…,B^c,Mc, such as the B-splines of the Function Spaces example. The basis of the form space is obtained by multiplying each of them with the basis k-form of its component, numbering first all basis forms of the first component, then those of the second one, and so on:

ϵik=B^1,iω1k,i=1,…,M1,ϵM1+ik=B^2,iω2k,i=1,…,M2,…

For a 1-form in 2D, the function space provides two sets of basis functions, {B^1,1,…,B^1,M1} and {B^2,1,…,B^2,M2}, and the basis of the form space is

ϵ11=B^1,1dx^1,…,ϵM11=B^1,M1dx^1,ϵM1+11=B^2,1dx^2,…,ϵM1+M21=B^2,M2dx^2.

For k=0 and k=n there is a single component, so a scalar space is enough: ϵi0=B^i and ϵin=B^idx^1∧⋯∧dx^n. For 0<k<n, which in 1D, 2D and 3D means (nk)=n components, a space with several components is built from scalar spaces with FunctionSpaces.DirectSumSpace((space_1, space_2, ...)), whose basis functions are numbered in exactly this way.

Form fields. Forms.FormField(form_space, coefficients, label) is the linear combination of the basis forms with the given coefficients:

uhk=∑i=1Muiϵik,M=M1+M2+….

The spaces of the different ranks do not have to be related. Choosing them so that the exterior derivative maps each space into the next one gives a de Rham complex, which is what makes discretizations stable; see De Rham Complexes. Here we only want to show how forms are built, so we use the same B-spline space for every component.

On a mapped geometry, the form lives on the manifold M, and the expressions above in x^ are its representation on the parametric domain, its pull-back by the mapping Φ of the Geometry example.

Components in canonical coordinates. Like geometries and function spaces, forms are evaluated element by element at points of the canonical element. Forms.evaluate returns the components of the form with respect to the canonical basis forms, the table above with x^i replaced by ξi. On element e, with lower corner (x^e,1,…,x^e,n) and lengths he,1,…,he,n, the element map x^i=x^e,i+he,iξi gives dx^i=he,idξi, so the components are multiplied by element lengths:

adx^i=ahe,idξi,adx^1∧dx^2=ahe,1he,2dξ1∧dξ2,…

A form given in the physical coordinates x is pulled back with the Jacobian Je of Φe. For a 1-form and, when m=n, an n-form,

∑j=1mfjdxj=∑i=1n(∑j=1mfj∂Φe,j∂ξi)dξi,fdx1∧⋯∧dxn=fdetJedξ1∧⋯∧dξn,

that is, the vector of canonical components of a 1-form is JeTf.

Proxies. To look at a form in the physical domain, it is converted to the quantity it represents, its proxy. With α the canonical components and g the metric of Φe:

  • a 0-form is a function, its own proxy;

  • an n-form αdξ1∧⋯∧dξn is represented by its density ρ=α/detg, which is its Hodge star ⋆ (introduced below). On an unmapped geometry, ρ=a for adx1∧⋯∧dxn;

  • a 1-form is represented by its vector proxy a=Jeg−1α, given by the sharp operator ♯ (g−1) followed by a push-forward to the physical domain (Je). The vector proxy of ∑jajdxj is (a1,…,am);

  • in 3D, a 2-form is represented by the vector proxy of its Hodge star, a 1-form.

Visualizing forms ​

Besides Mantis we use the LinearAlgebra and Printf standard libraries and, for one plot, GLMakie.

julia
using Mantis
using LinearAlgebra
using Printf
using GLMakie

Plot.export_form_fields_to_vtk(forms, filename; output_directory_tree, degree) writes one VTK file per form, named after filename and the label of the form, with the proxies described above. As in the Geometry example, each element is sampled with Lagrange cells of degree degree. We write the files to a temporary folder; replace output_dir by any folder of your choice. The figures in this example were rendered from these files with ParaView.

julia
output_dir = mktempdir()
"/tmp/jl_Zogktk"

1D: 0- and 1-forms ​

On a line there are only 0- and 1-forms, and both have a single component: they are both built from a scalar function space. We take the line [0,2] with 4 elements of the Geometry example,

julia
line = Geometry.create_cartesian_box((0.0,), (2.0,), (4,))

and, as in the Function Spaces example, the M=6 quadratic, C1 B-splines B^1,…,B^6 on it.

julia
B_1D = FunctionSpaces.create_bspline_space(line, (2,), (1,))

We use this space for both the 0-forms and the 1-forms. The geometry is unmapped, so x^=x, and the bases of the two form spaces are

ϵi0=B^i,ϵi1=B^idx,i=1,…,6.
julia
Λ⁰_1D = Forms.FormSpace(0, B_1D, "Λ⁰")
Λ¹_1D = Forms.FormSpace(1, B_1D, "Λ¹")

Both form spaces have one basis form per B-spline:

julia
println("number of basis 0-forms: ", Forms.get_num_basis(Λ⁰_1D))
println("number of basis 1-forms: ", Forms.get_num_basis(Λ¹_1D))
number of basis 0-forms: 6
number of basis 1-forms: 6

A form field is a form space together with a vector of coefficients, one per basis form: the field is the linear combination

uh0=∑i=16uiϵi0,vh1=∑i=16viϵi1.

For the 0-form we take as coefficients the Greville abscissae of the space, which, as shown in the Function Spaces example, give uh0=x. For the 1-form we take all coefficients equal to one: by the partition of unity of the B-splines, ∑iB^i=1, so

vh1=(∑i=16B^i)dx=dx.
julia
(coefficients_u⁰,) = FunctionSpaces.get_greville_points(B_1D)
coefficients_v¹ = ones(Forms.get_num_basis(Λ¹_1D))
u⁰_1D = Forms.FormField(Λ⁰_1D, coefficients_u⁰, "u⁰")
v¹_1D = Forms.FormField(Λ¹_1D, coefficients_v¹, "v¹")

Forms.evaluate(form, element_id, ξ) evaluates the form field on element element_id, at a collection of canonical points, ξ. The points are given as one of the point types of the Points module. The simplest one is Points.PointSet, which takes the coordinates of the points explicitly, one vector per direction. Here we take three points of the canonical element [0,1]:

julia
ξ = Points.PointSet([0.0, 0.5, 1.0])

On element 2, [0.5,1], the element map is x=0.5+0.5ξ. evaluate returns the canonical components of the form at these points. For the 0-form, this is its value,

uh0(x(ξ))=∑i=16uiB^i(x(ξ))=0.5+0.5ξ.

evaluate returns two objects. The first one is a vector with one entry per component of the form, each a vector with one value per point. The second one gives the indices of the evaluated forms. For a form space, these are the indices of the basis forms that are non-zero on the element; for a form field there is only one form, the field itself, so it is always [[1]].

julia
Forms.evaluate(u⁰_1D, 2, ξ)
([[0.5, 0.75, 1.0]], [[1]])

For the 1-form, vh1=dx=0.5dξ on element 2, so its canonical component is 0.5 at every point:

julia
Forms.evaluate(v¹_1D, 2, ξ)
([[0.5, 0.5, 0.5]], [[1]])

Visualization. For 0-forms in 1D, Mantis provides a Makie plot, Plot.plot_solution (since Makie exports a name Plot, we write Mantis.Plot):

julia
fig = Mantis.Plot.plot_solution((u⁰_1D,); title=L"u^0_h = x", ylabel=L"u^0_h")

Other forms are exported to VTK files:

julia
Mantis.Plot.export_form_fields_to_vtk(
    (u⁰_1D, v¹_1D), "forms_1D"; output_directory_tree=[output_dir], degree=4
)
Writing form 'u⁰' to file ...
Writing form 'v¹' to file ...

The figure shows the proxies stored in these files: the value of uh0 and the density of vh1, which is 1.

2D: 0-, 1- and 2-forms ​

In 2D, 0- and 2-forms have one component and 1-forms have two. We take the unit square [0,1]2 of the Geometry example, with 4×3 elements,

julia
square = Geometry.create_cartesian_box((0.0, 0.0), (1.0, 1.0), (4, 3))

and, as in the Function Spaces example, quadratic, C1 B-splines in both directions: 6 univariate B-splines B^i1 in the first direction and 5, B^j2, in the second one. Their M=6⋅5=30 products are numbered with a single index l, with the first direction running fastest:

B^l=B^i1B^j2,l=i+6(j−1),i=1,…,6,j=1,…,5.
julia
B_2D = FunctionSpaces.create_bspline_space(square, (2, 2), (1, 1))

We use this space for every component. The 1-form space has two components, so its function space is the direct sum of two copies of B_2D. The bases of the three form spaces are, for l=1,…,30,

ϵl0=B^l,ϵl1=B^ldx1,ϵ30+l1=B^ldx2,ϵl2=B^ldx1∧dx2.
julia
Λ⁰_2D = Forms.FormSpace(0, B_2D, "Λ⁰")
Λ¹_2D = Forms.FormSpace(1, FunctionSpaces.DirectSumSpace((B_2D, B_2D)), "Λ¹")
Λ²_2D = Forms.FormSpace(2, B_2D, "Λ²")
julia
println("number of basis 0-forms: ", Forms.get_num_basis(Λ⁰_2D))
println("number of basis 1-forms: ", Forms.get_num_basis(Λ¹_2D))
println("number of basis 2-forms: ", Forms.get_num_basis(Λ²_2D))
number of basis 0-forms: 30
number of basis 1-forms: 60
number of basis 2-forms: 30

We build the form fields

uh0=x1x2,vh1=x1dx1+x2dx2,wh2=(x1+x2)dx1∧dx2.

The Greville abscissae γ1,i and γ2,j of the two directions give the coordinates, x1=∑iγ1,iB^i1 and x2=∑jγ2,jB^j2. By the partition of unity in each direction, the coefficients γ1,iγ2,j, γ1,i and γ2,j of B^l then give x1x2, x1 and x2. So, with l=i+6(j−1), i=1,…,6 and j=1,…,5,

uh0=∑l=130ulϵl0,ul=γ1,iγ2,j,vh1=∑l=160vlϵl1,vl=γ1,i,v30+l=γ2,j,wh2=∑l=130wlϵl2,wl=γ1,i+γ2,j.

In the code, the index l runs with i fastest, which is the order in which Julia stores a matrix, so the coefficients are vectorized matrices of values at the points (γ1,i,γ2,j).

julia
γ₁, γ₂ = FunctionSpaces.get_greville_points(B_2D)
coefficients_u⁰ = vec([x₁ * x₂ for x₁ in γ₁, x₂ in γ₂])
coefficients_v¹ = vcat(vec([x₁ for x₁ in γ₁, x₂ in γ₂]), vec([x₂ for x₁ in γ₁, x₂ in γ₂]))
coefficients_w² = vec([x₁ + x₂ for x₁ in γ₁, x₂ in γ₂])
u⁰_2D = Forms.FormField(Λ⁰_2D, coefficients_u⁰, "u⁰")
v¹_2D = Forms.FormField(Λ¹_2D, coefficients_v¹, "v¹")
w²_2D = Forms.FormField(Λ²_2D, coefficients_w², "w²")

We export them to VTK files:

julia
Mantis.Plot.export_form_fields_to_vtk(
    (u⁰_2D, v¹_2D, w²_2D), "forms_2D"; output_directory_tree=[output_dir], degree=4
)
Writing form 'u⁰' to file ...
Writing form 'v¹' to file ...
Writing form 'w²' to file ...

The figure shows uh0, the vector proxy (x1,x2) of vh1, and the density of wh2.

3D: 0-, 1-, 2- and 3-forms ​

In 3D, 0- and 3-forms have one component, and 1- and 2-forms have three. We take the unit cube [0,1]3 of the Geometry example, with 4×3×2 elements,

julia
cube = Geometry.create_cartesian_box((0.0, 0.0, 0.0), (1.0, 1.0, 1.0), (4, 3, 2))

and trilinear, C0 B-splines on it: 5, 4 and 3 univariate B-splines B^i1, B^j2 and B^k3 in the three directions, whose Greville abscissae γ1,i, γ2,j and γ3,k are the breakpoints. Their M=5⋅4⋅3=60 products are numbered with the first direction running fastest:

B^l=B^i1B^j2B^k3,l=i+5(j−1)+20(k−1),i=1,…,5,j=1,…,4,k=1,…,3.
julia
B_3D = FunctionSpaces.create_bspline_space(cube, (1, 1, 1), (0, 0, 0))

The 1- and 2-form spaces use the direct sum of three copies of B_3D. With the basis forms of the table above, for l=1,…,60,

ϵl0=B^l,ϵl1=B^ldx1,ϵ60+l1=B^ldx2,ϵ120+l1=B^ldx3,ϵl3=B^ldx1∧dx2∧dx3,ϵl2=B^ldx2∧dx3,ϵ60+l2=B^ldx3∧dx1,ϵ120+l2=B^ldx1∧dx2.
julia
V_3D = FunctionSpaces.DirectSumSpace((B_3D, B_3D, B_3D))
Λ⁰_3D = Forms.FormSpace(0, B_3D, "Λ⁰")
Λ¹_3D = Forms.FormSpace(1, V_3D, "Λ¹")
Λ²_3D = Forms.FormSpace(2, V_3D, "Λ²")
Λ³_3D = Forms.FormSpace(3, B_3D, "Λ³")

As in 2D, we take as coefficients of each component its values at the points (γ1,i,γ2,j,γ3,k), which give

uh0=x1x2x3,vh1=x1dx1+x2dx2+x3dx3,ρh3=(x1+x2+x3)dx1∧dx2∧dx3,wh2=x2dx2∧dx3+x3dx3∧dx1+x1dx1∧dx2.
julia
γ₁, γ₂, γ₃ = FunctionSpaces.get_greville_points(B_3D)
x₁ = vec([x₁ for x₁ in γ₁, x₂ in γ₂, x₃ in γ₃])
x₂ = vec([x₂ for x₁ in γ₁, x₂ in γ₂, x₃ in γ₃])
x₃ = vec([x₃ for x₁ in γ₁, x₂ in γ₂, x₃ in γ₃])
u⁰_3D = Forms.FormField(Λ⁰_3D, x₁ .* x₂ .* x₃, "u⁰")
v¹_3D = Forms.FormField(Λ¹_3D, vcat(x₁, x₂, x₃), "v¹")
w²_3D = Forms.FormField(Λ²_3D, vcat(x₂, x₃, x₁), "w²")
ρ³_3D = Forms.FormField(Λ³_3D, x₁ .+ x₂ .+ x₃, "ρ³")

We export them to VTK files. The export of 2-forms in 3D is not supported yet (it writes zeros), so we export the Hodge star of wh2, a 1-form, whose vector proxy is the vector proxy of wh2.

julia
Mantis.Plot.export_form_fields_to_vtk(
    (u⁰_3D, v¹_3D, ★(w²_3D), ρ³_3D),
    "forms_3D";
    output_directory_tree=[output_dir],
    degree=4,
)
Writing form 'u⁰' to file ...
Writing form 'v¹' to file ...
Writing form 'star(w²)' to file ...
Writing form 'ρ³' to file ...

The figure shows, from left to right, uh0, the vector proxy (x1,x2,x3) of vh1, the vector proxy (x2,x3,x1) of wh2, and the density of ρh3. The arrows are colored by their length.

Analytical forms ​

A form can also be given by an analytical expression, for example an exact solution or a right-hand side: Forms.AnalyticalFormField(k, expression, geometry, label). The argument expression is a Julia function that takes the physical points x(1),…,x(P), as a matrix with one row per point and one column per coordinate, and returns a vector with one vector of values per component of the form, in the physical basis. For example, for the forms

f,∑j=1mfjdxj,fdx1∧⋯∧dxn,

of rank 0, 1 and n, it returns [f], [f1,…,fm] and [f], where each fj stands for the vector (fj(x(1)),…,fj(x(P))). Here m is the image dimension of the geometry, and n-forms require m=n. Analytical 2-forms in 3D are not supported yet.

The expression is defined in physical coordinates, but, like all forms in Mantis, an analytical form is evaluated in the canonical domain: when it is evaluated on an element, Mantis evaluates the expression at the physical points Φe(ξ) and pulls the result back automatically, with the formulas of Components in canonical coordinates.

As an example, the 1-form v1=x1dx1+x2dx2 on the square has (f1,f2)=(x1,x2):

julia
v¹_expression(x) = [x[:, 1], x[:, 2]]
v¹_exact = Forms.AnalyticalFormField(1, v¹_expression, square, "v¹ exact")

Since the B-splines reproduce linear functions, the finite element form vh1 of the previous section is equal to it, at any point. To check this on a grid of points, we use Points.TensorProductPoints, which takes one vector of coordinates per direction and forms all their combinations; see TensorProductPoints. Here it gives 3×2 points on each element:

julia
ξ_2D = Points.TensorProductPoints(([0.0, 0.3, 1.0], [0.2, 0.9]))
all(
    Forms.evaluate(v¹_exact, e, ξ_2D)[1] ≈ Forms.evaluate(v¹_2D, e, ξ_2D)[1] for
    e in 1:Geometry.get_num_elements(square)
)
true

Analytical forms are evaluated and exported like any other form.

L2 projection ​

The projection ​

The L2 inner product of two k-forms on a domain Ω is

(αk,βk)Ω=∫Ωαk∧⋆βk.

The L2 projection of a k-form fk onto a finite element form space Λhk is the form fhk∈Λhk closest to fk in the norm of this inner product. It is characterized by

(vk,fhk)Ω=(vk,fk)Ω∀vk∈Λhk.

Writing fhk=∑j=1Mcjϵjk and taking vk=ϵik gives a linear system for the coefficients,

∑j=1MMijcj=bi,Mij=(ϵik,ϵjk)Ω,bi=(ϵik,fk)Ω,i=1,…,M,

whose matrix M is the mass matrix of Λhk. Assemblers.solve_L2_projection(Λ, f, dΩ) assembles and solves this system with the quadrature rule dΩ, and returns fhk as a FormField.

Two forms on the unit square ​

We project the 0-form and the 1-form

f0=sin⁡(πx1)sin⁡(πx2),f1=sin⁡(πx1)cos⁡(πx2)dx1−cos⁡(πx1)sin⁡(πx2)dx2,

first on a coarse mesh, with linear B-splines on the unit square with 2×2 elements.

julia
coarse_square = Geometry.create_cartesian_box((0.0, 0.0), (1.0, 1.0), (2, 2))

The two forms are analytical forms on this geometry:

julia
f⁰_expression(x) = [@. sinpi(x[:, 1]) * sinpi(x[:, 2])]
f¹_expression(x) =
    [@.(sinpi(x[:, 1]) * cospi(x[:, 2])), @.(-cospi(x[:, 1]) * sinpi(x[:, 2]))]
f⁰_coarse = Forms.AnalyticalFormField(0, f⁰_expression, coarse_square, "f⁰")
f¹_coarse = Forms.AnalyticalFormField(1, f¹_expression, coarse_square, "f¹")

We create a B-spline space that is linear (p=1) and C0 in both directions,

julia
B_coarse = FunctionSpaces.create_bspline_space(coarse_square, (1, 1), (0, 0))

and the form spaces are built from it as in the 2D section:

julia
Λ⁰_coarse = Forms.FormSpace(0, B_coarse, "Λ⁰")
Λ¹_coarse = Forms.FormSpace(1, FunctionSpaces.DirectSumSpace((B_coarse, B_coarse)), "Λ¹")

The integrals are computed with a Gauss–Legendre quadrature rule with 4 points per direction on every element; see the Quadrature documentation:

julia
rule = Quadrature.tensor_product_rule((4, 4), Quadrature.gauss_legendre)
dΩ_coarse = Quadrature.StandardQuadrature(rule, Geometry.get_num_elements(coarse_square))

The projections are

julia
f⁰_h_coarse = Assemblers.solve_L2_projection(Λ⁰_coarse, f⁰_coarse, dΩ_coarse)
f¹_h_coarse = Assemblers.solve_L2_projection(Λ¹_coarse, f¹_coarse, dΩ_coarse)

Analysis.compute_error_total(f_h, f, dΩ) computes the L2 norm of the difference,

∥fhk−fk∥L2=(fhk−fk,fhk−fk)Ω1/2,

with the quadrature rule dΩ. Both forms must be defined on the same geometry, which is why we built the analytical forms on coarse_square.

julia
error_f⁰_coarse = Analysis.compute_error_total(f⁰_h_coarse, f⁰_coarse, dΩ_coarse)
error_f¹_coarse = Analysis.compute_error_total(f¹_h_coarse, f¹_coarse, dΩ_coarse)
@printf("coarse: L2 error of f⁰: %.2e, of f¹: %.2e\n", error_f⁰_coarse, error_f¹_coarse)
coarse: L2 error of f⁰: 6.26e-02, of f¹: 1.05e-01

We repeat the same steps on a fine mesh, with cubic (p=3), C2 B-splines on 12×12 elements and 6 quadrature points per direction.

julia
fine_square = Geometry.create_cartesian_box((0.0, 0.0), (1.0, 1.0), (12, 12))
f⁰_fine = Forms.AnalyticalFormField(0, f⁰_expression, fine_square, "f⁰")
f¹_fine = Forms.AnalyticalFormField(1, f¹_expression, fine_square, "f¹")
B_fine = FunctionSpaces.create_bspline_space(fine_square, (3, 3), (2, 2))
Λ⁰_fine = Forms.FormSpace(0, B_fine, "Λ⁰")
Λ¹_fine = Forms.FormSpace(1, FunctionSpaces.DirectSumSpace((B_fine, B_fine)), "Λ¹")
rule = Quadrature.tensor_product_rule((6, 6), Quadrature.gauss_legendre)
dΩ_fine = Quadrature.StandardQuadrature(rule, Geometry.get_num_elements(fine_square))
f⁰_h_fine = Assemblers.solve_L2_projection(Λ⁰_fine, f⁰_fine, dΩ_fine)
f¹_h_fine = Assemblers.solve_L2_projection(Λ¹_fine, f¹_fine, dΩ_fine)
error_f⁰_fine = Analysis.compute_error_total(f⁰_h_fine, f⁰_fine, dΩ_fine)
error_f¹_fine = Analysis.compute_error_total(f¹_h_fine, f¹_fine, dΩ_fine)
@printf("fine:   L2 error of f⁰: %.2e, of f¹: %.2e\n", error_f⁰_fine, error_f¹_fine)
fine:   L2 error of f⁰: 3.11e-06, of f¹: 4.24e-06

We export the exact forms and the two projections. The label of a form is the name of its field in the VTK file, as shown in ParaView, and is also appended to the file name. The coarse and fine projections have the same labels, inherited from their form spaces, so we export them with different file names.

julia
Mantis.Plot.export_form_fields_to_vtk(
    (f⁰_fine, f¹_fine), "projection_exact"; output_directory_tree=[output_dir], degree=4
)
Mantis.Plot.export_form_fields_to_vtk(
    (f⁰_h_coarse, f¹_h_coarse),
    "projection_coarse";
    output_directory_tree=[output_dir],
    degree=4,
)
Mantis.Plot.export_form_fields_to_vtk(
    (f⁰_h_fine, f¹_h_fine), "projection_fine"; output_directory_tree=[output_dir], degree=4
)

The figures compare the exact forms with the two projections. The coarse projection of f0 is bilinear on each element and misses the round peak, and the coarse 1-form only follows the vortex roughly. The fine projections cannot be told apart from the exact forms.

A curved geometry ​

Nothing changes on a mapped geometry: the analytical forms are given in physical coordinates and Mantis pulls them back. On the half annulus of the Geometry example, with quadratic, C1 B-splines on 4×12 elements, we repeat the same steps with the same expressions, now evaluated on 1≤|x|≤2, x2≥0.

julia
annulus = Geometry.create_annulus_sector((4, 12))
f⁰_annulus = Forms.AnalyticalFormField(0, f⁰_expression, annulus, "f⁰")
f¹_annulus = Forms.AnalyticalFormField(1, f¹_expression, annulus, "f¹")
B_annulus = FunctionSpaces.create_bspline_space(annulus, (2, 2), (1, 1))
Λ⁰_annulus = Forms.FormSpace(0, B_annulus, "Λ⁰")
Λ¹_annulus = Forms.FormSpace(1, FunctionSpaces.DirectSumSpace((B_annulus, B_annulus)), "Λ¹")
rule = Quadrature.tensor_product_rule((5, 5), Quadrature.gauss_legendre)
dΩ_annulus = Quadrature.StandardQuadrature(rule, Geometry.get_num_elements(annulus))
f⁰_h_annulus = Assemblers.solve_L2_projection(Λ⁰_annulus, f⁰_annulus, dΩ_annulus)
f¹_h_annulus = Assemblers.solve_L2_projection(Λ¹_annulus, f¹_annulus, dΩ_annulus)
error_f⁰_annulus = Analysis.compute_error_total(f⁰_h_annulus, f⁰_annulus, dΩ_annulus)
error_f¹_annulus = Analysis.compute_error_total(f¹_h_annulus, f¹_annulus, dΩ_annulus)
@printf("annulus: L2 error of f⁰: %.2e, of f¹: %.2e\n", error_f⁰_annulus, error_f¹_annulus)
annulus: L2 error of f⁰: 6.44e-02, of f¹: 1.03e-01
julia
Mantis.Plot.export_form_fields_to_vtk(
    (f⁰_annulus, f¹_annulus), "annulus_exact"; output_directory_tree=[output_dir], degree=4
)
Mantis.Plot.export_form_fields_to_vtk(
    (f⁰_h_annulus, f¹_h_annulus),
    "annulus_projection";
    output_directory_tree=[output_dir],
    degree=4,
)

Operations on forms ​

Exterior derivative, Hodge star and wedge product ​

The Forms module provides the operators of exterior calculus; see Operations on Forms. Mantis exports the most common ones, so they can be used without the Forms. prefix. We use three of them:

  • the exterior derivative d, which maps a k-form to a (k+1)-form. It does not depend on the metric, so it has the same expression in any coordinates. Mantis applies it to the canonical components; in 2D,

    dα=∂α∂ξ1dξ1+∂α∂ξ2dξ2,d(α1dξ1+α2dξ2)=(∂α2∂ξ1−∂α1∂ξ2)dξ1∧dξ2.

    In terms of proxies, it is the gradient on 0-forms and the scalar curl on 1-forms. For a finite element form it acts on the basis forms, for example duh0=∑iuidϵi0 with dϵi0=∑j∂B^i∂x^jdx^j;

  • the Hodge star ★ (typed \bigstar), which maps a k-form to an (n−k)-form and depends on the metric g, with entries gij and inverse g−1 with entries gij. In 2D, in canonical components,

    ⋆α=αdetgdξ1∧dξ2,⋆(αdξ1∧dξ2)=αdetg,⋆(α1dξ1+α2dξ2)=detg(−(g21α1+g22α2)dξ1+(g11α1+g12α2)dξ2).

    On the unit square, in the physical coordinates, these reduce to ⋆f=fdx1∧dx2 and ⋆(a1dx1+a2dx2)=−a2dx1+a1dx2, a rotation of the vector proxy by 90∘;

  • the wedge product ∧ (typed \wedge), which maps a k-form and an l-form to a (k+l)-form. It does not depend on the metric. In 2D,

    f∧(a1dx1+a2dx2)=fa1dx1+fa2dx2,(a1dx1+a2dx2)∧(b1dx1+b2dx2)=(a1b2−a2b1)dx1∧dx2,

    and the same expressions hold for the canonical components.

These operators do not compute anything when they are applied: d(f⁰_h) is an expression, which is evaluated when it is evaluated, exported or integrated. Expressions can be combined with each other and with +, - and multiplication by numbers. The exterior derivative of an analytical form is not available, so we give the exact results as analytical forms.

For the forms of the previous section, the exact results are

df0=πcos⁡(πx1)sin⁡(πx2)dx1+πsin⁡(πx1)cos⁡(πx2)dx2,df1=2πsin⁡(πx1)sin⁡(πx2)dx1∧dx2,⋆f0=sin⁡(πx1)sin⁡(πx2)dx1∧dx2,⋆f1=cos⁡(πx1)sin⁡(πx2)dx1+sin⁡(πx1)cos⁡(πx2)dx2,f0∧f1=sin⁡(πx1)sin⁡(πx2)(sin⁡(πx1)cos⁡(πx2)dx1−cos⁡(πx1)sin⁡(πx2)dx2),f1∧df0=π(sin2⁡(πx1)cos2⁡(πx2)+cos2⁡(πx1)sin2⁡(πx2))dx1∧dx2.
julia
df⁰_expression(x) =
    [@.(π * cospi(x[:, 1]) * sinpi(x[:, 2])), @.(π * sinpi(x[:, 1]) * cospi(x[:, 2]))]
df¹_expression(x) = [@. 2π * sinpi(x[:, 1]) * sinpi(x[:, 2])]
star_f¹_expression(x) =
    [@.(cospi(x[:, 1]) * sinpi(x[:, 2])), @.(sinpi(x[:, 1]) * cospi(x[:, 2]))]
f⁰f¹_expression(x) = [f⁰_expression(x)[1] .* component for component in f¹_expression(x)]
f¹_wedge_df⁰_expression(x) =
    [@.(π * (sinpi(x[:, 1])^2 * cospi(x[:, 2])^2 + cospi(x[:, 1])^2 * sinpi(x[:, 2])^2))]

Comparing with the exact results ​

We apply each operation to the coarse and fine projections fh0 and fh1 of the previous section, and compute the L2 error with respect to the exact result. Each operation is given by its name, the expression applied to the projections, and the rank and expression of the exact result.

julia
for (mesh, geometry, f⁰_h, f¹_h, dΩ) in (
    ("coarse", coarse_square, f⁰_h_coarse, f¹_h_coarse, dΩ_coarse),
    ("fine", fine_square, f⁰_h_fine, f¹_h_fine, dΩ_fine),
)
    println(mesh)
    for (name, computed, rank, expression) in (
        ("d f⁰", d(f⁰_h), 1, df⁰_expression),
        ("d f¹", d(f¹_h), 2, df¹_expression),
        ("★ f⁰", ★(f⁰_h), 2, f⁰_expression),
        ("★ f¹", ★(f¹_h), 1, star_f¹_expression),
        ("f⁰ ∧ f¹", f⁰_h ∧ f¹_h, 1, f⁰f¹_expression),
        ("f¹ ∧ d f⁰", f¹_h ∧ d(f⁰_h), 2, f¹_wedge_df⁰_expression),
    )
        exact = Forms.AnalyticalFormField(rank, expression, geometry, name)
        error = Analysis.compute_error_total(computed, exact, dΩ)
        @printf("  %-10s L2 error: %.2e\n", name, error)
    end
end
coarse
  d f⁰       L2 error: 9.87e-01
  d f¹       L2 error: 1.11e+00
  ★ f⁰       L2 error: 6.26e-02
  ★ f¹       L2 error: 1.05e-01
  f⁰ ∧ f¹    L2 error: 7.83e-02
  f¹ ∧ d f⁰  L2 error: 4.69e-01
fine
  d f⁰       L2 error: 2.34e-04
  d f¹       L2 error: 2.16e-04
  ★ f⁰       L2 error: 3.11e-06
  ★ f¹       L2 error: 4.24e-06
  f⁰ ∧ f¹    L2 error: 3.81e-06
  f¹ ∧ d f⁰  L2 error: 1.03e-04

All errors decrease under refinement. The results that involve an exterior derivative (d f⁰, d f¹ and f¹ ∧ d f⁰) have larger errors, because they contain derivatives of the projections.

Expressions are exported like any other form. We export three of the computed forms on the fine mesh: the gradient dfh0, the curl dfh1 and fh1∧dfh0.

julia
Mantis.Plot.export_form_fields_to_vtk(
    (d(f⁰_h_fine), d(f¹_h_fine), f¹_h_fine ∧ d(f⁰_h_fine)),
    "operations";
    output_directory_tree=[output_dir],
    degree=4,
)

Summary and outlook ​

In this example we learned that:

  • a form space Forms.FormSpace(k, space, label) combines a function space with (nk) components with the basis k-forms, and a form field Forms.FormField(form_space, coefficients, label) is a linear combination of its basis forms. Spaces with several components are direct sums of scalar spaces;

  • Forms.AnalyticalFormField(k, expression, geometry, label) defines a form by an expression in physical coordinates;

  • forms are evaluated in canonical coordinates, and visualized through their proxies: values, densities and vector proxies;

  • Assemblers.solve_L2_projection computes the L2 projection of a form onto a form space, and Analysis.compute_error_total its L2 error;

  • d, ★ and ∧ build expressions that are evaluated, exported and integrated like forms.

The functions used in this example are:

taskfunction
form spaceForms.FormSpace(k, space, label)
multi-component spaceFunctionSpaces.DirectSumSpace(spaces)
form fieldForms.FormField(form_space, coefficients, label)
analytical formForms.AnalyticalFormField(k, expression, geometry, label)
evaluationForms.evaluate
VTK exportPlot.export_form_fields_to_vtk
0-form plot in 1DPlot.plot_solution
L2 projectionAssemblers.solve_L2_projection
L2 errorAnalysis.compute_error_total
operationsd, ★, ∧
